title: Roots with gutturals

objectives.can: Parse verbs with a guttural as first, second or third root consonant and explain their changed vowels.

explanation.summary: Four consonants, alef, he, het and ayin, are called gutturals, and they cannot behave like other consonants: they refuse a doubling dagesh, they cannot carry a simple shewa, and they like the a-vowel. A verb whose root contains one is still regular in its plan, but its vowels change in a few predictable ways, and once you know the cause you can read them at sight.

sections.heading: One cause, three consequences
body: The gutturals (א ה ח ע) are made at the back of the mouth. Hebrew spelling treats them differently from the other consonants in three ways. First, they are not doubled: a guttural never takes a doubling dagesh, so where the pattern of a verb would double one, the vowel before it is lengthened instead (compensatory lengthening), or sometimes left short. Second, a guttural at the beginning of a syllable that would take a simple shewa takes a composite shewa instead (ֲ ֱ ֳ), a shewa with a short vowel's colour in it. Third, gutturals attract a-vowels: where an ordinary verb has o or i, a guttural verb often has a.
Everything in this lesson is an application of those three habits to a verb you already know how to parse. Nothing here is a new conjugation.

sections.heading: The traditional names, once
body: Old grammars name a root class by the place of its weak consonant, counting the three root consonants against the three letters of the old model root (pe, ayin, lamed): pe is the first consonant, ayin the second and lamed the third. A root with a guttural first is called pe-guttural, with a guttural second ayin-guttural, with a guttural third lamed-guttural. The names are only labels; this lesson uses plain 'first', 'second' and 'third' guttural, and notes the label when you will meet it in reference books.
The same label is used for the other weak classes in the lessons that follow: pe-nun (first nun), pe-yod (first yod), and so on.

sections.heading: Guttural first: composite shewa
body: A regular verb puts a simple shewa under its first consonant whenever a syllable break falls there. A guttural cannot bear a simple shewa, so it takes a composite one. In the Qal yiqtol the prefix is then pointed with a as well: compare the prefix of יַעֲמֹד with the hireq that an ordinary verb has. The same happens in the wayyiqtol (וַיַּעֲבֹד), after a preposition on the infinitive (לַעֲבֹד), and in the qatal when an ending that begins with a consonant pulls the stress forward (עֲזַבְתֶּם).

Notice what does not change. When the first guttural can hold a full vowel with the shewa falling on the next consonant, the form looks perfectly regular: עִבְדוּ, the plural imperative, and עָזְבוּ, the third plural qatal, have a full vowel under the guttural and a simple shewa under the second consonant. The composite shewa appears only where an ordinary root would have a simple shewa under its first consonant.

The third masculine plural wayyiqtol of the same root shows both patterns side by side: וַיַּעַבְדוּ, with a full patah under the ayin, and וַיַּעֲבֹד, with a composite shewa. Which one you get depends only on whether the next syllable is open or closed.

sections.heading: Guttural first: the alef verbs, and the verb that lengthens
body: When the first guttural is alef, a small group of very common verbs, among them אָמַר and אָכַל, takes ō in the yiqtol prefix: יֹאכַל, and in the wayyiqtol וַיֹּאמֶר and וַיֹּאכְלוּ. The alef is silent, and the prefix and alef together make one long syllable. This is why 'and he said' never looks like a regular wayyiqtol. Other first-alef verbs follow the ordinary a-vowel pattern: וַיֶּאֱהַב, from אָהַב, has the segol and the composite shewa of a first guttural.

In the Niphal, the first consonant is normally doubled after the prefix. A guttural cannot be doubled, so the vowel before it is lengthened to make up for it: the Niphal yiqtol of אָכַל is יֵאָכֵל, with a long vowel under the prefix and no dagesh in the alef. The Hiphil of חָזַק, הֶחֱזִיק, shows the composite shewa after a short segol prefix, where a regular verb would have a hireq and a simple shewa.

sections.heading: Guttural second and third: a-vowels and the furtive patah
body: A second-guttural verb keeps its pattern but prefers a: where the Qal yiqtol of a regular verb has o, בָּחַר has יִבְחַר and שָׁאַל has וַיִּשְׁאַל. When an ending adds a vowel after the guttural, it takes a composite shewa rather than a simple one: צָעֲקָה, שָׁאֲלוּ.

A third-guttural verb has two signs. The stem vowel is usually a, as in יִשְׁלַח (an ordinary verb would have o), and the imperative is שְׁמַע, not a form with o. And when a long vowel stands before a final ח or ע, a very short a is pronounced between the vowel and the guttural: this is the furtive patah, written under the guttural but read before it. It appears in the participle שֹׁמֵעַ and in the infinitive construct לִשְׁמֹעַ. When an ending is added, the guttural is no longer final and the furtive patah disappears: compare שֹׁמֵעַ with the forms that have an ending in the lesson on Qal participles.

misunderstandings: A composite shewa is not a new vowel and does not add a syllable. It is the shewa that a guttural has to use, and it is pronounced very briefly. The prefix a in יַעֲמֹד does not make this a Hiphil: look at the whole form, the stem vowel and the sense.
The furtive patah is read before the guttural, although it is written beneath it. It is not part of the root, and it is not a sign of a different stem; it disappears when a vowel ending follows.

Not every verb with a guttural has all of these changes. A root with a guttural in the first place has the first-position changes, not those of the second or third; the same root can have a guttural in the first and the third place at once, and then both appear. Read each form for the position that is actually in play.
וַיֹּאמֶר is not 'and he will say'. It is a wayyiqtol, a narrative past; the ō in the prefix is the sign of a first-alef verb, not of the future.

deeper.heading: Why a?
body: Grammarians have long explained the guttural's liking for a by the place where it is articulated: the back of the throat is close to the position of the mouth for a. This is a phonetic explanation of a tendency, not a law, and the Hebrew texts show exceptions in every class. For reading, it is enough to treat the tendency as a pattern that helps you recognise a root.

deeper.heading: The letter resh
body: The letter ר is not counted among the gutturals, but it also refuses a doubling dagesh. In a Piel or Niphal with ר as a root consonant you may therefore see the same lengthening of the vowel before it. This lesson does not treat ר as a guttural root class; you will meet its effects as an exception to doubling.

examples.analysis: Five forms of two roots with a first guttural. לַעֲבֹד is an infinitive construct of עָבַד with the preposition ל: the ayin takes a composite shewa, and the preposition is pointed with patah in agreement. תַעֲבֹדוּן and נַעֲבֹד are yiqtol forms with the same composite shewa after the prefix. עָבְדוּ is a third plural qatal, regular in shape because the shewa falls on the second consonant. בַּחֲרוּ is an imperative of בָּחַר, a second-guttural verb: the composite shewa stands under the het because an ending follows.

examples.analysis: חֲזַק and וֶאֱמָץ are two imperatives side by side. In both, the first consonant is a guttural (ח, א) and takes a composite shewa where a regular imperative would have a simple one. The first is from חָזַק, the second from אָמַץ, another first-guttural verb. Together they mean 'be strong and courageous'.

reading.why: Joshua's challenge at Shechem: 'serve', 'choose', 'leave' and 'listen' come back again and again, so עָבַד, בָּחַר, עָזַב and שָׁמַע appear in many forms, together with the first-alef verb אָמַר.
